pike-place.name: Pike Place Market & the Gum Wall
pike-place.blurb: Seattle's 1907 public market under the red "PUBLIC MARKET CENTER" neon sign: flying fish, Rachel the bronze pig, the original Starbucks and the Gum Wall in Post Alley.

spawn.note: Pike St at 1st Ave, looking down Pike St at the sign + clock (classic arrival view).

extent.description: Pike St from 1st Ave down to the Main Arcade corner (sign, clock, Rachel, Pike Place Fish), Pike Place north (brick, pedestrian since 2025 trial) past Beecher's, Le Panier, Piroshky Piroshky and the original Starbucks (1912 Pike Pl) to Victor Steinbrueck Park; Post Alley south under the market to the Gum Wall / Market Theater; MarketFront plaza (2017) west over the bluff. Lower levels (Down Under) and Hillclimb are optional interiors/edges.
extent.walkable_surfaces: Pike Place (brick, living street), Pike St (brick/sett), Post Alley (concrete/paving stones/sett, partly building passage), MarketFront deck (concrete), Steinbrueck Park (grass + brick).
extent.edges: East: 1st Ave building line (cars + buses as backdrop). West: Western Ave / bluff railing over Alaskan Way and Elliott Bay. South: Post Alley beyond Gum Wall (fence/stairs). North: Virginia St.
extent.vertical: Pike Place level ~30 m NAVD88 at Pike St (USGS EPQS 30.1 m at 47.6085,-122.3405); bluff drops ~20 m to Western Ave/Alaskan Way. Post Alley at the Gum Wall is ~1 storey below Pike St (stairs + ramp under the Pike St bridge/arcade).

structures.form: Long low shed-roofed arcade on the west side of Pike Place; open-fronted daystalls under a continuous canopy; rooftop on the Pike St corner carries the PUBLIC MARKET CENTER sign + clock; timber posts, ceiling with exposed beams and hanging bulbs; fluorescent/neon vendor signs inside.
materials: dark green painted window frames and canopy fascia
concrete floor with inlaid tiles (donor tiles)
structures.details: Pike Place Fish Market stall at the Pike St corner (orange overalls, ice-covered fish table, hanging "PIKE PLACE FISH" sign); Rachel the pig stands on the brick in front under the sign; "MEET THE PRODUCER" lettering stretched along the arcade fascia (Market creed).

structures.name: "PUBLIC MARKET CENTER" neon sign and clock
structures.form: Rooftop sign on a black steel scaffold with X-bracing above the Main Arcade corner at Pike St: THREE stacked rows of individual sheet-metal block capitals — PUBLIC (top), MARKET (middle, widest), CENTER (bottom) — each letter a deep brick-red box letter with red neon tube outlines; a large round clock sits to the right of MARKET/PUBLIC (black ring, face glowing red-orange at night, numerals 1–12, red hands). Thin horizontal steel rails carry each row.
structures.ref_check: Verified against refs/sea-spots/pike-place/Public_Market_Center_Sign_Seattle_United_States_Unsplash_.jpg (CC0) and Pike_Place_Market_Entrance.jpg (2012, CC BY-SA 3.0).
structures.details: Built 1937 per the Market (other sources say 1927/1928); designed by architect Andrew Willatsen; one of the largest neon signs on the West Coast when installed; restored and repainted with enamel in 2022. A separate red neon "FARMERS MARKET" sign by Willatsen is at Pike Place & Pine St.

sources.url: https://www.pikeplacemarket.org/?p=27746 (Pike Place Market: neon signs / Meet the Producer)

structures.name: Rachel the Piggy Bank (Georgia Gerber, 1986)
structures.form: Life-size bronze sow piggy bank with coin slot on top of the head, on a low base; bronze hoof prints in the pavement lead to it; plaque "Market Foundation Piggy Bank. Made possible by a gift from Fratelli's Ice Cream, August 17, 1986".
materials: bronze, polished gold where touched (snout, ears, back)
structures.copyright_note: Sculpture by Georgia Gerber (1986), still in copyright: model as a generic stylised bronze pig, do not texture from photos.

structures.name: Gum Wall (Market Theater, Post Alley)

dims.note: 2024: 54 ft long × 8 ft high, ~180 pieces/brick; earlier reached 15–20 ft

structures.form: Both brick walls of Post Alley under the market, beside the Market Theater box office, covered with thousands of multicoloured chewed gum blobs, gum strings, notes, business cards; dripping texture; small heart shapes; Market Theater marquee/door. Alley ~4 m wide, sett/paving-stone floor, stairs up to Pike St at the north end.
materials: chewing gum (pink, green, blue, white, yellow, red)
structures.details: Started ~1991–1993 by Unexpected Productions theatre-goers; allowed to stay ~1999; fully steam-cleaned Nov 2015 (first time in 20 years); Jan 2024 Pete Carroll gum mural. Use a decal/instanced-blob system (thousands of small spheroids, 1–3 cm) with density 180/brick at 0.5–2 m height.

vegetation: Flower stalls (Hmong growers) with large tulip / dahlia / peony bouquets in buckets — strongest colour block in the arcade (seasonal)

Window boxes and hanging baskets on Post Alley
furniture: OSM inside polygon: 25 bicycle racks, 14 waste baskets, 3 recycling, 3 post boxes, 2 info points, 1 drinking fountain, toilets (2), 6 street lamps, 5 bollards (extract file furniture{})

Hand carts and dollies of crafters at the daily roll call (time unverified)

lighting.day: Mostly overcast soft light; arcade interior darker with warm incandescent bulbs and fluorescent tubes over stalls.
lighting.night: Neon sign + clock glow red (#FF3B2F); FARMERS MARKET neon orange with green border; MEET THE PRODUCER bulbs; holiday light sculptures (carrot, pear, trees) in December and illuminate the corner; many smaller neon signs on lower levels; stalls close ~5–6 pm, shops later; acorn lamps warm white 2700 K.

backdrop: 1st Ave historic blocks (Hahn Building 1908, Broderick, Liberty, Eitel) to the east
The Emerald tower (2020, 134 m) and Newmark Tower (24 storeys) behind
West: Elliott Bay, Great Wheel (Pier 57), ferries, the Olympic Mountains on clear days
South: Harbor Steps towers, Four Seasons

crowd.density: Very high 10:00–16:00 (up to 10,000/day at the fish stall in summer); queue of 20–40 at original Starbucks; moderate early morning (vendors setting up, daily roll call), sparse after 6 pm except Gum Wall photographers and diners.
activities: buskers (guitar, accordion, piano on a cart) at designated chalk-circle spots
tourists photographing the sign from Pike St
gum sticking and selfies at the Gum Wall

sounds: Fishmongers' call-and-response chant and splat of fish caught in paper
Gulls (Elliott Bay) and ferry horn in the distance

plaques.title: Since 1907
plaques.text: Pike Place Market opened on August 17, 1907, and is one of the oldest continuously operated public farmers' markets in the United States.

plaques.title: The sign
plaques.text: The Public Market Center clock and sign went up on a new 1937 roof; designed by architect Andrew Willatsen, it was one of the largest neon signs on the West Coast.

plaques.title: Rachel
plaques.text: Rachel, a 550 lb bronze piggy bank by Georgia Gerber, was dedicated on the market's 79th birthday in 1986; donations fund the Market's social services.

plaques.title: Flying fish
plaques.text: Pike Place Fish Market (founded 1930) nearly went bankrupt in 1986, then became "world famous" by throwing fish; up to 10,000 people watch on a summer day.

plaques.title: The Gum Wall
plaques.text: Gum started appearing here in the 1990s while theatre-goers waited in line; as of 2024 the wall is 54 ft long and 8 ft high, about 180 pieces of gum per brick.

plaques.title: Original Starbucks
plaques.text: Starbucks opened in 1971 at 2000 Western Ave and moved to 1912 Pike Place in 1977, where it still uses the original siren logo.

interaction.primary: Stick gum on the Gum Wall: buy a gum pack at a stall (or from inventory), aim at the wall, choose a colour; the blob persists for the session (instanced decal). Bonus: arrange 5 blobs into a heart for an achievement.
secondary: Order a fish at Pike Place Fish: the crew chants the order and throws a salmon over the counter — catch it with a timed click (QTE).
Drop a coin in Rachel (counter increments; plaque thanks you).
Join the queue at the original Starbucks (time-skip) and get a cup prop.
interaction.safety: No real brand logos are needed for gameplay; use generic "fish market" and coffee storefront if branding is a concern.

iconic.frame: Looking down Pike St: the PUBLIC MARKET CENTER sign and clock above the arcade corner, fish stall and crowds below; best at blue hour when the neon glows.

dialogueGeneral.usage: Pedestrian set for the Seattle and Bellevue driving districts and as filler in every spot. ctx: greeting|bumped|photographed|idle|spot|rain|honked_at|near_miss; non-English lines carry orig+lang with English text.

tone.note: "Seattle Freeze": locals are described as "very polite but not particularly friendly" to strangers — keep local NPC lines courteous, brief, low-key; few unprompted chats.
Washington ranked 48th of 50 states for extraversion (2008 study cited by Wikipedia) — locals default to nods, "sorry", "you're good".

Honking is rare and seen as rude: ~3 in 4 Northwest drivers said they rarely or never honk (PEMCO 2017); attitudes softened by 2021 (65% say honking at least somewhat appropriate). NPC reaction to player honking near spots: surprised/disapproving, not aggressive.
Coffee culture: Seattle drinks more coffee than any other US city; espresso small talk is a safe icebreaker.
Rain talk is universal small talk; locals rarely use umbrellas (hoods/rain shells) — common local self-image, unsourced folklore: keep light.

Visitors: Canada was 73% of Seattle's 2.4 M international visitors in 2024; then China, India, UK, South Korea, Germany, Japan, Australia, France, Taiwan — languages used: English, French (Québec), Mandarin, Hindi, Korean, German, Japanese, Spanish (domestic + Latin America).
Indigenous art (totems, Salish Welcome): staff/guides speak respectfully; no jokes about sacred objects.
Guardrails: no stereotypes, accents written phonetically, slurs, politics or alcohol jokes about any group; tourists are curious and happy, locals helpful-but-reserved.
